blocks.text: The chapter does not settle exactly what tongues sounded like. It describes speech directed to God, mysterious to hearers, capable of interpretation, and able to edify the speaker; Paul's practical concern is whether the gathered church can understand and be built up. Even the contrast between spirit and understanding keeps both together rather than making reflection a spiritual defect.

Prophecy receives preference in the assembly because it addresses people for upbuilding, encouragement, and consolation, whereas uninterpreted tongues do not instruct the gathered community. The same chapter makes prophecy accountable: two or three may speak, others weigh what is said, and a speaker yields when another receives a revelation. A claimed spiritual word therefore does not end communal discernment.

The Isaiah quotation and the statement about tongues as a sign sit beside two contrasting visitor scenes: undifferentiated tongues can make outsiders judge the gathering mad, while intelligible prophecy can expose what is hidden and turn a visitor toward God. The closing assembly instructions therefore emphasize shared participation, intelligibility, peace, and ordered turns. These controls explain the practice without settling every question about the phenomenon itself.

The textual history of verses 34-35 deserves care: the verses appear in extant Greek witnesses, while some Western witnesses place them after verse 40. Within the chapter's sequence, keeping silent is associated with an uninterpreted tongue speaker, a prophet displaced by another revelation, and women or wives in the disputed passage. That pattern makes both effortless deletion and an unqualified permanent ban on women's speech too simple; the precise activity and scope remain contested.

sections.title: Love and the Wider Gift Discussion

blocks.text: Chapter 13 stands between the gift discussions of chapters 12 and 14. In that literary setting, love corrects rivalry, self-display, and knowledge used competitively; it is not simply a detached treatment of romantic sentiment. Reading chapter 14 alongside that intervening argument keeps spiritual activity connected to the common good rather than to status or spectacle.

The description of love in chapter 13 names patience, kindness, truth, and a refusal to insist on one's own way. As a surrounding control on the gift discussion, those traits help a reader see why spiritual activity cannot be separated from truthful, noncoercive treatment of other people.

Acts presents Pentecost as recognizable languages or dialects heard by an international gathering. That scene can illuminate the larger question of intelligible speech, but the supplied context does not make it an exact definition of what happened at Corinth; the relation between these early Christian speech phenomena remains debated.
